messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Musician
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 45

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the therapy office with his guitar case leaning against the wall beside him—a habit, he explains, since he never knows when a gig might come up. At fifty, he still has the lean frame of someone who's spent decades hunched over an instrument, though his posture has grown more guarded in recent years. His fingers tap against his thigh in an unconscious rhythm as he speaks, a nervous percussion that never quite stops.

Six years ago, Marcus was performing regularly at jazz clubs across the city. He was respected in his community, known for his technical skill and his ability to read a room—to sense what people needed to hear. His life felt full then, even after his divorce three years prior. Music had always been his refuge, the one place where the noise in his head could transform into something beautiful.

Then he met someone at one of his performances. A woman who came to every show, who always requested the same song, who began waiting for him after sets. At first, Marcus thought it was flattering. She was attentive, interested in his music, seemed to understand something about him that others didn't. He was lonely. He let her in.

Within weeks, the attention became suffocating. She showed up at his apartment unannounced. She called repeatedly when he didn't answer. She created social media accounts impersonating him, contacting other musicians he knew. When he tried to end things, she escalated. She waited outside his apartment building. She followed him to gigs. She sent him photographs taken from outside his windows—images of him sleeping, showering, moving through his own home. The police became involved. A restraining order was issued. But the violation had already taken root in his nervous system.

Now, six years later, Marcus still checks his locks multiple times before bed. He still scans crowds at venues, mapping exits and identifying faces. When someone approaches him after a performance, his chest tightens. His hands shake. The joy he once felt playing in front of an audience has been replaced by hypervigilance. He notices every detail—the woman in the third row who makes eye contact too long, the man who lingers by the stage door, the phone number texted from an unknown account.

He's stopped performing at smaller venues where he can't control access. He's turned down lucrative gigs because they require him to be visible, to be known, to be findable. The guitar case beside him is less about spontaneous opportunity and more about the fact that he rarely stays in one place for long. He moves apartments every eight months. He keeps his phone number unlisted. He's become someone who exists in the margins of his own life.

The worst part, Marcus says, isn't the fear itself—it's that he can't distinguish between real danger and the phantom of it anymore. A notification on his phone sends him into a spiral. A repeated number in his call log triggers hours of obsessive checking. His mind has learned to see threat everywhere, and his body responds with the same intensity whether the danger is real or imagined. He's exhausted by his own vigilance.

He still plays, but differently now. Alone in his apartment, late at night, when he knows no one is watching. The music is technically perfect but something has been stolen from it—the openness, the generosity, the sense of connection that once made him feel alive. He's become a musician who no longer performs, a man defined by what he's learned to fear.
